finding.claim: The /fetch handler passes the `target` query parameter straight to http.Get with no validation. An attacker can make the server request internal hosts, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254) or localhost services, and the full response body is returned to them. This is a full-read SSRF.
finding.source: r.URL.Query().Get("target") at main.go:15 (the `target` query parameter on /fetch)
finding.sink: http.Get(target) at main.go:16, with the response body copied back to the client by io.Copy at main.go:22

trace.note: The /fetch route is registered with the fetch handler. There is no authentication or middleware.
target is read from the attacker-controlled query string
target is passed unchanged to http.Get. Go's default client follows redirects and the URL scheme is not restricted.
The upstream response body is streamed back to the attacker, so the SSRF is non-blind

finding.guards_checked: No scheme check, no host allowlist (the `allowed` map is only used in safeFetch), no IP or DNS validation, and no egress filtering in the code. Error text is also returned to the client at main.go:18, which leaks connection details. No auth on the route.

verdict.reason: main.go:15 reads the attacker-controlled `target` and main.go:16 passes it unvalidated to http.Get, and main.go:22 returns the body. The `allowed` check exists only in safeFetch (main.go:27), and /fetch is registered at main.go:41 with no auth or middleware.
